abstract.p: Accurate remaining useful life (RUL) prediction of rolling bearings is essential for predictive maintenance and reliable operation of industrial rotating machinery. However, variations in operating conditions introduce substantial differences in vibration characteristics and degradation patterns, limiting the applicability of models trained under individual operating conditions. This study investigates a multi-source transfer learning approach for bearing RUL prediction across different operating conditions. A framework termed deep residual shrinkage network with multi-source weighted screening (DRSN-MW) was developed by integrating a deep residual shrinkage network with multi-source domain screening, subdomain alignment, and physical monotonicity constraints. An adaptive feature extraction module was constructed to capture degradation characteristics from vibration signals, while weighted extension correlation and dynamic time warping (DTW) were combined to identify source domains with similar degradation patterns. Degradation-stage partitioning and entropy-weighted local maximum mean discrepancy (LMMD) were employed to align source and target features within corresponding degradation stages. Physical monotonicity and decision consistency constraints were further incorporated to regulate the predicted RUL trajectories. The framework was evaluated using the 2012 Prognostics and Health Management (PHM2012) bearing dataset and Xi’an Jiaotong University–Sumyoung (XJTU-SY) bearing dataset under single-source and multi-source transfer scenarios. Average mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 0.126 and 0.129 and root mean square errors (RMSEs) of 0.150 and 0.156 were obtained on the two datasets, respectively. On the PHM2012 dataset, the proposed method reduced the average root mean square error by 33.6% compared with the strongest baseline in the reported comparison. The results indicate that combining source-domain screening with degradation-stage alignment and physical constraints can improve RUL prediction across operating conditions. The proposed framework provides a data-driven approach to bearing health prognostics and predictive maintenance in industrial rotating machinery.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Rolling element bearings are essential components of industrial rotating machinery and are widely used in manufacturing equipment, power generation systems, and other mechanical installations [1]. During prolonged operation, bearings are subjected to varying rotational speeds, mechanical loads, and thermal conditions, which may accelerate material degradation and eventually lead to mechanical failure. As components particularly susceptible to wear and fatigue, their operating conditions directly influence equipment reliability, operational safety, and maintenance costs [2]. Bearing-related failures account for a substantial proportion of unexpected machinery downtime in industrial applications [3]. Consequently, accurate prediction of bearing remaining useful life (RUL) is an important element of condition-based maintenance (CBM), allowing maintenance activities to be planned according to equipment degradation rather than predetermined service intervals [4].

Despite considerable progress in machinery health prognostics, reliable RUL prediction under varying operating conditions remains difficult. Industrial rotating machinery frequently operates under changing rotational speeds, mechanical loads, and temperatures, resulting in variations in vibration responses and degradation characteristics [5]. These changes may alter both the statistical distributions of monitoring signals and the progression of bearing deterioration. Moreover, obtaining complete run-to-failure data for every operating condition is generally impractical because accelerated life testing requires considerable time and experimental resources [6], [7]. Consequently, the available degradation records often cover only a limited range of operating conditions, while data collected from different machines or operating environments may exhibit substantial distribution discrepancies. Models developed using data from a single operating condition may therefore produce unreliable predictions when applied to previously unseen conditions [8]. Addressing these discrepancies is essential for developing RUL prediction methods suitable for industrial predictive maintenance.

Transfer learning provides a means of addressing this problem by transferring degradation knowledge from operating conditions with sufficient labeled data to target conditions for which labeled observations are limited or unavailable [9], [10]. Within this field, deep domain adaptation (DDA) has received considerable attention because it allows transferable representations to be learned directly from monitoring signals. Existing DDA approaches can broadly be divided into feature distribution alignment methods and adversarial adaptation methods, depending on how discrepancies between source and target domains are addressed.

Feature alignment methods generally seek to reduce statistical differences between source and target representations while retaining information relevant to the prediction task. Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) has been widely adopted for this purpose, and studies by Zhang et al. [11] and Wang et al. [12] have provided methodological foundations for deep feature learning and machinery prognostics. Zhu et al. [13] further investigated transfer learning for bearing monitoring under different operating conditions. Nevertheless, alignment based primarily on global feature distributions may not adequately account for differences among successive stages of bearing degradation. Early degradation is often characterized by relatively weak changes in vibration responses, whereas advanced deterioration may involve more pronounced fault-related impulses and rapidly changing signal characteristics. These stages may exhibit different degradation mechanisms and feature distributions [14]. Consequently, global alignment alone may produce inappropriate correspondence between source and target samples at different degradation stages, particularly when their degradation trajectories progress at different rates [15].

Adversarial domain adaptation offers another approach by learning feature representations that are less sensitive to differences between operating conditions [16], [17], [18]. Related studies have investigated adversarial training, attention mechanisms, and feature disentanglement for machinery fault diagnosis and health monitoring. For example, Li et al. [19] examined deep-learning-based representations for rotating machinery, while Hu et al. [20] investigated feature disentanglement for bearing RUL prediction under different working conditions. Although these approaches provide useful strategies for cross-domain feature learning, adversarial optimization may introduce additional training complexity and sensitivity to model configuration. A further difficulty arises when several source domains are available. Multi-source transfer learning methods [21], [22], [23] can incorporate information from multiple operating conditions, but differences in degradation patterns mean that not every source domain contributes equally to the target prediction task. Source selection based only on general distribution similarity may overlook differences in degradation progression, increasing the possibility of negative transfer when poorly matched source domains are included in model training.

Recent research has also examined self-supervised learning and pretrained representations as alternatives for reducing dependence on labeled degradation data. Liu et al. [24] investigated learning strategies for bearing fault prediction, while Zhou and Barati Farimani [25] developed a Transformer-based pretraining approach for transferable bearing fault representations. Such developments indicate the potential of representation learning for extracting useful information from vibration measurements. However, when target-domain pseudo-labels are used to guide adaptation, errors introduced during the initial prediction stage may propagate through subsequent training iterations [26]. Studies by Chen et al. [27] and Peng et al. [28] have also explored feature alignment and domain adaptation in related learning problems, providing further methodological references for cross-domain representation learning. Despite these developments, the integration of degradation characteristics and physically meaningful constraints into transfer learning remains an important issue in machinery prognostics [29]. In particular, models optimized primarily according to prediction error may produce fluctuations or locally increasing RUL estimates that are inconsistent with the expected progression of bearing degradation. Such behavior can complicate the interpretation of predicted degradation trajectories and their use in industrial maintenance planning.

The preceding studies indicate three issues that require further attention in cross-condition bearing RUL prediction. First, global domain adaptation may overlook differences between early and advanced degradation stages, resulting in incomplete alignment of degradation-related features. Second, the selection and combination of multiple source domains require greater consideration of degradation trend similarity to limit the influence of unrelated operating conditions. Third, prediction models need to account for the temporal consistency of bearing degradation so that estimated RUL trajectories remain physically reasonable. These issues are closely related: unsuitable source-domain selection can introduce inconsistent degradation information, while insufficient stage-wise alignment and unconstrained regression may further increase prediction errors under changing operating conditions.

To address these issues, this study developed a deep residual shrinkage network with multi-source weighted screening (DRSN-MW) for cross-condition RUL prediction of rolling bearings. The framework combined noise-robust feature extraction, weighted source-domain screening, degradation-stage alignment, and physically constrained prediction within a unified transfer learning architecture. Its main contributions are summarized as follows.

p.p: A noise-robust degradation feature extraction module was developed using a DRSN with channel-adaptive threshold adjustment and multi-scale feature fusion. The module was designed to suppress noise-related responses while retaining vibration features associated with different stages of bearing degradation under varying operating conditions.

A multi-source domain screening strategy was established by combining entropy-weighted extension correlation with dynamic time warping (DTW). The strategy evaluated both feature similarity and temporal degradation characteristics to identify source domains more closely related to the target operating condition, thereby reducing the influence of potentially unsuitable source data during knowledge transfer.

A degradation-stage-aware subdomain alignment method was developed using adaptive stage partitioning, Mix-up-based feature recombination, and entropy-weighted local MMD. The method aligned source and target representations within corresponding degradation stages rather than relying exclusively on global distribution matching, allowing differences in stage-dependent degradation characteristics to be considered during model adaptation.

Decision consistency regularization and a physical monotonicity constraint were incorporated into the prediction objective to regulate the outputs of multiple source-domain regression heads. These constraints were intended to reduce inconsistencies among regression predictions and discourage increases in estimated RUL along the degradation trajectory, supporting more stable and physically consistent bearing life predictions.

sec.p: The proposed framework was evaluated using the 2012 Prognostics and Health Management (PHM2012) bearing dataset and Xi’an Jiaotong University–Sumyoung (XJTU-SY) bearing dataset under single-source and multi-source cross-condition transfer scenarios. Prediction accuracy, the contribution of individual model components, and resistance to signal noise were examined through comparative experiments and ablation studies. sec.title: 2.1. Problem description
sec.p: Cross-condition RUL prediction involves transferring degradation knowledge from one or more operating conditions to a target condition with a different data distribution. Domain adaptation generally assumes that the marginal distributions of the source and target domains differ,
\[ P\left(X_s\right) \neq P\left(X_t\right) \]
while their conditional distributions remain sufficiently similar,
\[ P\left(Y_s \mid X_s\right) \approx P\left(Y_t \mid X_t\right) \]

to permit knowledge transfer. In bearing prognostics, however, changes in rotational speed, mechanical load, and degradation progression may affect both the statistical characteristics of vibration signals and their relationships with the corresponding RUL values. Consequently, alignment of global feature distributions alone may not adequately preserve the degradation information required for accurate prediction.

As illustrated in Figure 2a, global domain adaptation attempts to reduce the overall distribution discrepancy between source and target features without explicitly distinguishing individual degradation stages. This may cause samples representing different health conditions to become incorrectly aligned in the latent feature space, particularly when the source and target bearings exhibit different degradation rates. Such misalignment can affect the learned regression function and introduce errors into the predicted RUL trajectories.

Subdomain adaptation addresses this limitation by considering the internal structure of the degradation process during feature alignment. Rather than treating all observations as belonging to a single distribution, the bearing degradation process is divided into corresponding health stages, and feature distributions are aligned within these stages. As shown in Figure 2b, this approach seeks to reduce inter-domain discrepancies while retaining the distinctions between successive degradation states. Stage-wise alignment is therefore particularly relevant to cross-condition bearing prognostics, where the characteristics of early degradation and advanced fault development may differ substantially.

sec.title: 2.2. Deep residual shrinkage networks
sec.p: The DRSN [30] is a residual learning architecture designed to extract informative features from signals affected by noise and interference. It incorporates adaptive soft-thresholding into residual blocks, allowing low-magnitude feature responses to be attenuated during feature extraction. This characteristic makes DRSN suitable for vibration-based machinery health monitoring, where fault-related components may be obscured by background vibration and measurement noise.

The principal component of DRSN is the residual shrinkage building unit (RSBU), which combines residual connections with a channel-wise thresholding mechanism. Unlike the conventional rectified linear unit (ReLU), which sets negative inputs to zero, soft-thresholding suppresses feature responses whose absolute magnitudes fall below a specified threshold and reduces the magnitudes of the remaining responses. Nevertheless, the relationship between feature magnitude and useful degradation information depends on the characteristics of the input signal; consequently, the threshold must be adjusted according to the learned feature representations.

A distinguishing characteristic of DRSN is that the threshold is estimated adaptively rather than assigned as a fixed parameter. In the conventional channel-wise DRSN structure, global average pooling (GAP) is applied to obtain channel descriptors, which are subsequently processed by fully connected layers to generate channel-dependent threshold coefficients. The resulting threshold vector allows different feature channels to undergo different degrees of shrinkage according to their learned responses.

For bearing RUL prediction, this mechanism provides a foundation for extracting degradation-related features from vibration signals collected under different operating conditions. However, the conventional threshold estimation structure may introduce additional parameters, and its channel interactions can be further refined. Accordingly, the DRSN-MW framework developed in this study incorporates an efficient channel attention (ECA) mechanism and multi-scale feature extraction, as described in Section 3.2. sec.title: 3.1. Overview of the proposed framework
sec.p: The proposed DRSN-MW was developed to predict the RUL of rolling bearings across different operating conditions. The framework integrates noise-robust degradation feature extraction, source-domain screening, degradation-stage-based feature alignment, and physically constrained regression within a multi-source transfer learning architecture. Labeled degradation data from multiple operating conditions are used to learn transferable representations, while unlabeled observations from the target condition are incorporated during domain adaptation. As illustrated in Figure 4, the framework comprises five interconnected modules.

sec.p:
(1) Shared noise-robust feature extraction. A modified DRSN was employed as the shared feature extractor
F ( )
to obtain degradation-related representations from raw bearing vibration signals. Adaptive soft-thresholding was combined with channel attention and multi-scale feature extraction to attenuate noise-related responses while retaining information associated with bearing deterioration. The resulting feature representations were used for source-domain screening, degradation-stage identification, and subsequent cross-domain alignment. The detailed network structure and feature extraction procedure are presented in Section 3.2.

(2) Multi-source weighted extension-based screening. A source-domain screening module was constructed to evaluate the relevance of available labeled source domains to the target operating condition. The evaluation combined weighted extension correlation, which characterizes differences in feature distributions, with entropy-weighted DTW, which measures similarities between temporal degradation trajectories. Feature weights were determined from information entropy to account for differences in the contributions of individual degradation features. Source domains with relatively low similarity to the target condition were excluded, while the selected domains were retained to form the source-domain subset

. This procedure was intended to limit negative transfer caused by combining degradation data from dissimilar operating conditions. The screening method is described in Section 3.3.

(3) Degradation-stage partitioning. A subdomain partition network was introduced to distinguish the principal stages of bearing degradation. Following degradation onset detection, the degradation process was divided into two subdomains representing early degradation and the subsequent fault stage. The partition network was trained using labeled source-domain observations and produced stage predictions for source samples and stage probability distributions for unlabeled target samples. These outputs provided stage-related information for sample recombination and conditional feature alignment, allowing the adaptation process to account for differences in degradation progression between operating conditions.

(4) Subdomain feature alignment with sample recombination. A stage-aware alignment module was developed to reduce feature distribution discrepancies between the selected source domains and the target domain. Rather than aligning all samples within a single global feature distribution, the proposed method considered corresponding degradation stages separately. Within each subdomain, Mix-up-based feature recombination was employed to generate intermediate representations between source and target samples, thereby regularizing the regression function across domains. An entropy-weighted local maximum mean discrepancy (LMMD) loss was also introduced to measure stage-conditional distribution differences, with additional weighting assigned to samples and stages exhibiting greater uncertainty. The combination of sample recombination and conditional distribution alignment was designed to preserve degradation-stage information while reducing cross-condition feature discrepancies. The complete alignment procedure is detailed in Section 3.4.

(5) Decision optimization with consistency and physical constraints. RUL estimation was performed using multiple source-domain regression heads, denoted by

. The prediction model was trained using a supervised regression objective based on labeled source-domain samples, together with decision consistency and physical monotonicity regularization. The decision consistency term penalized discrepancies among predictions generated by different regression heads for the same target-domain observations. The monotonicity constraint penalized increases in predicted RUL between successive observations along a bearing degradation trajectory, reflecting the non-increasing nature of remaining life during continued operation. These terms were incorporated into the overall optimization objective alongside the subdomain alignment loss to regulate prediction behavior under varying operating conditions. The corresponding loss functions and optimization procedure are presented in Section 3.5.

Through these modules, DRSN-MW establishes a unified procedure for extracting degradation-related features, identifying relevant source domains, aligning stage-dependent representations, and estimating bearing RUL under previously unseen operating conditions. The framework combines information from multiple degradation datasets while accounting for differences in operating conditions and temporal degradation characteristics. Its overall architecture is illustrated in Figure 4, and the implementation of each component is described in the following sections.

sec.title: 3.2. Deep residual shrinkage network-based noise-robust feature extraction module
sec.p: The DRSN provides the feature extraction backbone of the proposed DRSN-MW framework. Its adaptive soft-thresholding mechanism allows low-magnitude feature responses to be attenuated during signal processing, making it suitable for extracting degradation-related information from bearing vibration signals affected by background noise and operating-condition variations [30]. However, the conventional DRSN-CW architecture estimates channel-wise thresholds primarily through global feature aggregation and fully connected transformations. Although this mechanism provides adaptive noise suppression, the estimation of channel importance can be further refined by explicitly modeling interactions between neighboring feature channels.

To obtain more informative degradation representations for cross-condition RUL prediction, two modifications were introduced into the DRSN feature extraction module. First, an ECA mechanism was incorporated into the threshold estimation path to model local cross-channel dependencies and regulate the soft-thresholding operation. Second, a multi-scale feature extraction structure was constructed to combine representations obtained from different depths of the residual network. The resulting features were subsequently used for source-domain screening, degradation-stage partitioning, and cross-domain feature alignment.

sec.title: 3.2.1 Improved threshold path structure
sec.p: The conventional DRSN-CW architecture employs channel-dependent soft thresholds to attenuate noise-related feature responses. These thresholds are commonly estimated using GAP followed by fully connected layers. Although effective for adaptive feature shrinkage, this approach introduces additional parameters and does not explicitly preserve local relationships between neighboring channels during threshold estimation.

To address these limitations, the efficient channel attention network (ECA-Net) [32] was incorporated into the residual shrinkage blocks. ECA-Net uses one-dimensional convolution along the channel dimension to model local cross-channel interactions without introducing a dimensionality-reduction operation. The convolutional kernel size is determined according to the number of feature channels, allowing the attention mechanism to adjust its interaction range to the network structure.

sec.title: 3.3. Multi-source domain weighted extension-based screening module
sec.p: The selection of appropriate source domains is an important step in cross-condition bearing RUL prediction. Although degradation data collected under different operating conditions may contain transferable information, differences in rotational speed, mechanical load, and degradation progression can reduce the relevance of individual source domains to the target condition. Combining source data without considering these differences may introduce inconsistent degradation information and increase the risk of negative transfer.

To address this issue, a multi-source weighted extension-based screening module was developed to evaluate the relevance of available source domains before cross-domain feature alignment. The module combines feature-distribution assessment based on extension theory with temporal degradation similarity measured using entropy-weighted DTW. Information entropy is used to determine the relative contributions of individual features, while extension-based deviation analysis identifies differences between source-domain characteristics and the feature ranges observed in the target domain.

The screening procedure consisted of four stages: degradation-related feature extraction and entropy quantification, entropy-based feature weight calculation, extension correlation evaluation, and source-domain selection using entropy-weighted DTW. The selected source domains are subsequently used for subdomain alignment and RUL regression, as described in Sections 3.4 and 3.5.

sec.title: 3.3.1 Feature extraction and entropy quantification

By incorporating feature weighting into the extension neural network, W-ENN allows differences in the contributions of individual characteristics to be considered during correlation evaluation. This principle provides a useful basis for evaluating the relative importance of degradation-related features in cross-condition bearing analysis.

In the proposed DRSN-MW framework, the feature weighting principle was adopted to quantify the information content of degradation representations extracted by the DRSN module. Rather than using the original vibration measurements directly, the screening procedure operated on the learned feature representations, which contain information extracted from different network depths. The resulting source-domain subset provided the training data for the stage-aware adaptation module described in Section 3.4, with the aim of reducing the influence of poorly matched operating conditions on RUL prediction.

sec.title: 3.4. Construction of the subdomain alignment module
3.4.1 Architecture of the subdomain alignment module
sec.p: Domain adaptation aims to reduce discrepancies between source and target feature distributions while preserving information relevant to the prediction task. In cross-condition bearing RUL prediction, however, the degradation process is characterized by distinct stages with different vibration responses and temporal characteristics. Conventional global alignment methods may reduce the overall distribution discrepancy without adequately preserving the correspondence between samples at similar degradation stages. As a result, observations representing different levels of deterioration may become incorrectly aligned, affecting the regression function learned for the target operating condition.

To address this limitation, a degradation-stage-aware subdomain alignment module was incorporated into the proposed DRSN-MW framework. The module divided the bearing degradation process into two subdomains, representing early degradation and the subsequent fault stage. Feature alignment was then performed within corresponding degradation stages rather than across the entire source and target distributions. This approach was intended to retain stage-related information while reducing feature discrepancies caused by differences in operating conditions.

The two-stage partition was adopted to provide a relatively simple representation of degradation progression without introducing an excessive number of stage boundaries. The overall architecture is illustrated in Figure 6.

caption.title: Workflow of the proposed degradation-stage-aware subdomain alignment module

sec.p: The module consists of three interconnected components.

Adaptive degradation-stage partitioning. An initial degradation point was identified to distinguish the degradation period from the preceding healthy operation. The remaining degradation process was subsequently divided into early degradation and fault stages. A stage classification network was trained using labeled source-domain observations, while probabilistic stage assignments were generated for unlabeled target-domain samples. These assignments provided the stage information required for conditional feature alignment.

Cross-domain feature recombination. A feature-level Mix-up strategy was employed to generate intermediate representations between source and target samples assigned to corresponding degradation stages. By restricting sample recombination to the same degradation stage, the method was designed to reduce inappropriate interpolation between observations representing substantially different health conditions. The generated features were used to regularize the regression function across operating conditions.

Entropy-weighted subdomain alignment. LMMD was employed to measure differences between source and target feature distributions within individual degradation stages. Sample-level uncertainty and stage-level entropy were incorporated into the alignment objective to adjust the contributions of different observations and degradation stages. This procedure placed greater emphasis on regions where stage assignments were less certain.

Together, these components provided a stage-aware adaptation procedure that combined degradation point detection, probabilistic stage classification, feature recombination, and conditional distribution alignment.

sec.title: 4.1.1 Data preprocessing
sec.p: Bearing vibration signals collected under different operating conditions may exhibit substantial variations in amplitude and statistical distribution because of differences in rotational speed, mechanical load, and degradation progression. Such variations can affect feature extraction and reduce the consistency of representations learned from different operating conditions. Accordingly, a preprocessing procedure was applied before the vibration measurements were introduced into the DRSN-MW framework.

Following the degradation onset detection procedure described in Section 3.4.2, vibration observations corresponding to the identified degradation period were extracted for subsequent analysis. Min–max normalization was then applied to scale the signal amplitudes and reduce differences in numerical magnitude among the observations. The normalized vibration amplitude was calculated as

Min–max normalization reduces differences in numerical scale but does not, by itself, eliminate the statistical distribution discrepancies between operating conditions. sec.title: 4.1.3 Hyperparameter settings and implementation details
sec.p: The proposed DRSN-MW framework was implemented using PyTorch. Bayesian optimization was employed to determine the training hyperparameters within predefined search ranges. The batch size was searched between 16 and 64, the number of training epochs between 60 and 200, the weight decay between 0.001 and 0.1, and the initial learning rate between 0.0001 and 0.01.

The selected configuration consisted of 150 training epochs, a batch size of 64, an initial learning rate of 0.0001, and a weight decay of 0.001. The AdamW optimizer was used to update the trainable network parameters through backpropagation. A dropout rate of 0.2 was adopted in the relevant network layers, and ReLU was used as the activation function. The sliding-window length was set to 30.
The principal training parameters are summarized in Table 2.

caption.title: Hyperparameter settings for DRSN-MW training

sec.p: The same overall training configuration was used as the basis for the cross-condition transfer experiments described in the following sections. The experimental evaluation considered both single-source and multi-source transfer scenarios to examine the predictive behavior of DRSN-MW under different combinations of source and target operating conditions.

sec.title: 4.2. Dataset case 1: institute of electrical and electronics engineers prognostics and health management 2012 challenge dataset
4.2.1 Dataset description
sec.p: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) 2012 Challenge bearing dataset [34] was used to evaluate the proposed DRSN-MW framework under different operating conditions. The dataset was collected using the PRONOSTIA experimental platform, which was designed for accelerated bearing degradation testing. The platform allows bearing vibration responses to be monitored throughout the degradation process under specified rotational speeds and radial loads. The experimental arrangement is shown in Figure 8.

caption.title: PRONOSTIA experimental platform used for accelerated bearing degradation testing

sec.p: The dataset contains vibration measurements collected from bearings operated under three conditions. Horizontal and vertical vibration signals were acquired using two DYTRAN 3035B accelerometers at a sampling frequency of 25.6 kHz, with measurements recorded at intervals of 10 s.

The operating conditions differed in rotational speed and applied load, providing a basis for investigating the influence of operating-condition changes on the transferability of degradation representations. The corresponding experimental settings are listed in Table 3.

caption.title: Operating conditions of the IEEE PHM 2012 bearing dataset

sec.p: The differences in rotational speed and load produce distinct vibration characteristics and degradation trajectories, making the dataset suitable for evaluating cross-condition RUL prediction methods. In the present study, the three operating conditions were treated as separate domains, and transfer learning tasks were constructed by assigning different conditions to the source and target domains.

sec.title: 4.2.2 Prediction task design
sec.p: Six transfer learning tasks were constructed to evaluate DRSN-MW under different source-domain configurations. Tasks A–C represented single-source transfer scenarios, in which labeled degradation data from one operating condition were used to predict the RUL of bearings operating under another condition. Tasks D–F represented multi-source transfer scenarios, in which labeled data from two operating conditions were available for transfer to a third condition.

For each task, vibration observations from two bearings in each source condition were used as labeled training data. Two bearings from the target condition provided unlabeled observations for domain adaptation, while a separate target-domain bearing was reserved for testing. Target-domain RUL labels were not used during model training.
The task configurations are presented in Table 4.

caption.title: Cross-condition transfer learning task configurations for the PHM2012 dataset

sec.p: The single-source tasks were used to examine transfer between individual operating conditions, whereas the multi-source tasks evaluated whether combining degradation information from two conditions could reduce prediction errors on the target domain.

This experimental design provided a basis for comparing source-domain configurations while maintaining a separation between labeled source-domain training data, unlabeled target-domain adaptation data, and target-domain test observations.

sec.title: 4.2.3 Analysis of remaining useful life prediction results on the phm2012 dataset
sec.p: The prediction performance of DRSN-MW was evaluated across the six transfer learning tasks described in Section 4.2.2. MAE, RMSE, and Score were calculated for each task, and the results are summarized in Table 5.

caption.title: RUL prediction performance of DRSN-MW on the PHM2012 dataset

sec.p: The results showed that DRSN-MW maintained relatively low prediction errors across the six evaluated transfer scenarios. The average MAE and RMSE were 0.126 and 0.150, respectively, while the average Score was 0.987. Among the single-source tasks, Task C produced the lowest MAE and RMSE values of 0.138 and 0.154, respectively. Task B yielded the largest prediction errors, with an MAE of 0.145 and an RMSE of 0.157.

The multi-source tasks generally produced lower prediction errors than the corresponding single-source tasks. The average MAE decreased from approximately 0.141 for Tasks A–C to 0.111 for Tasks D–F, representing a relative reduction of approximately 21.3%. The average RMSE decreased from approximately 0.155 to 0.144. These differences indicate that incorporating degradation information from multiple operating conditions was associated with improved prediction performance under the evaluated task configurations.

Task F, which transferred information from operating conditions C1 and C2 to C3, achieved the lowest MAE of 0.104 and RMSE of 0.142, together with the highest Score of 0.992. Compared with the corresponding single-source transfer task C, the MAE decreased from 0.138 to 0.104, while the RMSE decreased from 0.154 to 0.142. Similar improvements were observed when comparing Tasks A and D and Tasks B and E, which shared the same target operating conditions but differed in the number of available source domains.

These results suggest that the use of multiple source domains can provide additional degradation information for RUL prediction when the selected domains contain transferable characteristics. The weighted screening mechanism was designed to evaluate source-domain relevance, while the stage-aware alignment procedure accounted for differences in degradation progression. The individual contributions of these components are examined further through the ablation experiments presented in Section 4.2.4.

From an industrial maintenance perspective, the observed reduction in prediction errors is relevant to situations in which complete run-to-failure records are unavailable for every operating condition. The experimental results indicate the potential of transferring degradation knowledge from previously monitored bearings to equipment operating under different loads and rotational speeds. However, the present evaluation was conducted using accelerated bearing test data, and its applicability to industrial equipment operating under more variable field conditions requires further investigation.

sec.title: 4.2.4 Ablation study
sec.p: An ablation study was conducted to examine the contributions of the principal components of the proposed DRSN-MW framework to cross-condition bearing RUL prediction. Starting from the conventional DRSN, additional components were introduced sequentially to assess changes in prediction performance. These components included degradation-stage-aware subdomain alignment, adaptive threshold adjustment, extension-based source-domain screening, and the decision optimization and physical constraints incorporated into the complete DRSN-MW framework.
The experiments were conducted using the six transfer learning tasks defined in Section 4.2.2. Prediction performance was evaluated using MAE, RMSE, and Score. The results are presented in Table 6.

caption.title: Ablation results for the proposed DRSN-MW framework on the PHM2012 dataset

sec.p: The results showed a progressive reduction in prediction errors as additional components were incorporated into the baseline model. The conventional DRSN produced an average MAE of 0.343 and an average RMSE of 0.439. After introducing subdomain alignment, these values decreased to 0.275 and 0.357, respectively. The corresponding Score increased from 0.864 to 0.898. This improvement suggests that accounting for degradation-stage information during feature alignment was associated with more accurate predictions across the evaluated operating conditions.

The subsequent incorporation of adaptive threshold adjustment further reduced the average MAE from 0.275 to 0.249 and the average RMSE from 0.357 to 0.344. This result is consistent with the intended role of channel-adaptive feature shrinkage in controlling the influence of noise-related responses. The additional improvement was smaller than that observed after introducing subdomain alignment, indicating that the two modifications contributed differently within the sequential experimental configuration.

After extension-based source-domain screening was introduced, the average MAE decreased to 0.173 and the average RMSE to 0.242, while the Score increased to 0.956. The reduction in prediction errors suggests that selecting source domains according to feature similarity and degradation trajectory characteristics can improve the relevance of information transferred to the target operating condition. However, because the modules were introduced sequentially, the observed improvement reflects the combined configuration rather than an isolated measurement of the screening module.

The complete DRSN-MW framework achieved an average MAE of 0.126, an average RMSE of 0.150, and an average Score of 0.987. Relative to the baseline DRSN, the average MAE and RMSE decreased by approximately 63.3% and 65.8%, respectively. The complete model also produced the lowest prediction errors among the evaluated configurations for all six transfer tasks.

The additional reduction in errors between the source-screening configuration and the complete DRSN-MW model was consistent with the intended role of decision consistency and physical monotonicity regularization. These constraints were designed to reduce disagreements among source-domain regression heads and discourage increases in predicted RUL along the degradation trajectory. Nevertheless, the reported error metrics do not independently establish the degree to which the predicted trajectories satisfied the monotonicity constraint.
The changes in MAE, RMSE, and Score across the evaluated configurations are further illustrated in Figure 9.

caption.title: Prediction performance of successive DRSN-MW configurations in the ablation study: (a) MAE; (b) RMSE; (c) Score

sec.p: As shown in Figure 9, the sequential introduction of additional components was associated with progressively lower prediction errors and higher Score values. The improvement was observed across both single-source and multi-source transfer tasks, suggesting that the combined architecture was effective under the operating-condition combinations considered in this study.

Overall, the ablation results indicate that the complete DRSN-MW configuration provided better prediction performance than the evaluated partial configurations. The findings support the use of degradation-stage alignment, adaptive feature extraction, source-domain screening, and constrained regression within a unified cross-condition bearing prognostics framework.

sec.title: 4.2.5 Comparison with other methods
sec.p: To assess the predictive performance of the proposed DRSN-MW framework relative to existing transfer learning approaches, comparative experiments were conducted using the six cross-condition transfer tasks defined in Section 4.2.2. The comparison included multi-prompt alignment (MPA) [35], style adaptation and uncertainty estimation (SAUE) [36], dynamic transfer (DRT) [37], and disentangling representation and adaptation network (DRANet) [38].

These methods represent different approaches to cross-domain representation learning and adaptation. MPA employs prompt-based alignment, SAUE considers adaptation and uncertainty estimation, DRT addresses multi-source domain adaptation, and DRANet separates representation learning from domain adaptation. Although these approaches were not originally developed specifically for bearing RUL prediction, they provide relevant methodological references for examining transfer learning under distribution shifts.

The original experimental design reported a common feature extraction architecture and parameter configuration for the compared methods. Such a configuration is intended to reduce differences arising from the feature extraction backbone. The reported MAE, RMSE, and Score values for the six transfer tasks are summarized in Table 7.

caption.title: Comparison of RUL prediction performance among transfer learning methods on the PHM2012 dataset

sec.p: The results showed that DRSN-MW achieved lower MAE and RMSE values than the compared methods across all six transfer tasks. Its average MAE and RMSE were 0.126 and 0.150, respectively, while the average Score reached 0.987. Among the comparison methods, DRANet achieved the lowest average prediction errors, with an MAE of 0.178 and an RMSE of 0.226.

Relative to DRANet, DRSN-MW reduced the average MAE by approximately 29.2% and the average RMSE by 33.6%. The average Score increased from 0.943 to 0.987, corresponding to an absolute increase of 0.044 and a relative increase of approximately 4.7%.

The performance differences were observed in both single-source and multi-source transfer scenarios. For example, in Task A, DRSN-MW achieved an RMSE of 0.155, compared with 0.253 for DRANet. In Task F, the corresponding RMSE values were 0.142 and 0.215. These results indicate that DRSN-MW produced smaller prediction errors under the evaluated operating-condition combinations.

The observed differences may be associated with the integration of several complementary mechanisms within DRSN-MW. The source-domain screening procedure was designed to limit the transfer of poorly matched degradation information, while subdomain alignment considered differences between early and advanced degradation stages. The decision consistency and monotonicity constraints further regulated the regression outputs. The ablation results in Section 4.2.4 provide additional evidence that the complete configuration was associated with lower prediction errors than the evaluated partial configurations.
For a visual comparison, the MAE, RMSE, and Score values of the five methods across the six transfer tasks are presented in Figure 10.

caption.title: Comparison of RUL prediction performance among transfer learning methods across six PHM2012 tasks

sec.p: As illustrated in Figure 10, DRSN-MW produced the lowest MAE and RMSE values in each task. Its Score values were also higher than those of the compared methods across the evaluated scenarios. The relatively small differences in prediction errors among the six tasks suggest that the proposed framework maintained consistent performance within the tested range of rotational speeds and mechanical loads.

These findings are relevant to industrial predictive maintenance because degradation data are often collected from machines operating under different conditions. A transfer learning method capable of using historical degradation information while accounting for operating-condition differences may reduce dependence on complete labeled degradation records for every target condition.

Nevertheless, the present comparison was conducted using accelerated bearing degradation datasets. The reported results therefore establish comparative performance under the specified experimental conditions rather than demonstrating field deployment performance in industrial machinery.

Overall, the comparative results indicate that DRSN-MW achieved lower prediction errors than the evaluated transfer learning methods on the PHM2012 dataset. The combination of source-domain screening, degradation-stage alignment, and constrained regression provides a plausible explanation for the observed differences, although the contribution of each mechanism should be interpreted in conjunction with the ablation results.

sec.title: 4.2.6 Visualization of feature distributions
sec.p: To examine the changes in feature distributions before and after domain adaptation, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) [39] was employed to visualize the high-dimensional degradation representations extracted by the shared feature extraction network. Task D, which involved transferring degradation information from operating conditions C2 and C3 to C1, was selected for visualization. The feature representations were projected into a two-dimensional space to illustrate differences in the relative distributions of source-domain and target-domain observations.

The visualization results are presented in Figure 11. Figure 11a shows the feature distributions before domain adaptation, while Figure 11b presents the corresponding distributions after applying the proposed DRSN-MW framework.

caption.title: t-SNE visualization of bearing degradation feature distributions for Task D: (a) before domain adaptation; (b) after domain adaptation

sec.p: Before adaptation, the source-domain and target-domain observations occupied relatively distinct regions of the two-dimensional embedding, as shown in Figure 11a. This separation indicated differences in the extracted feature representations under the evaluated operating conditions. Such differences are consistent with the changes in vibration characteristics and degradation progression associated with variations in rotational speed and mechanical load. When source and target observations exhibit different feature distributions, transferring a regression model without adaptation may introduce errors in the estimated RUL.

After applying DRSN-MW, the projected feature distributions showed greater overlap between the source and target domains, as illustrated in Figure 11b. The separation among observations originating from different operating conditions was reduced, and the feature representations appeared more closely distributed within the embedded space. This change was consistent with the intended effect of the proposed cross-domain adaptation procedure.

Several components of DRSN-MW may have contributed to the observed distribution changes. First, the modified DRSN feature extractor employed channel-adaptive soft-thresholding and multi-scale feature fusion to obtain degradation-related representations from vibration measurements. Second, the weighted source-domain screening module evaluated the relevance of available source conditions using feature characteristics and temporal degradation similarity. Third, entropy-weighted LMMD was used to reduce distribution discrepancies between corresponding degradation stages. The stage-consistent Mix-up procedure further introduced interpolated feature representations during model training.

Together, these mechanisms were designed to reduce operating-condition-dependent variations while retaining information relevant to the progression of bearing degradation. The greater overlap observed after adaptation was consistent with this objective.

Nevertheless, the interpretation of t-SNE results requires some caution. Because t-SNE is a nonlinear dimensionality-reduction method, distances and apparent cluster overlap in the two-dimensional embedding do not directly quantify distribution discrepancies in the original high-dimensional feature space. Accordingly, the visualization provides qualitative evidence of changes in the learned representations rather than an independent quantitative measure of domain alignment.

The visualization results, considered together with the prediction errors reported in Table 5 and the ablation results in Table 6, suggest that the proposed adaptation procedure produced representations more suitable for cross-condition RUL prediction under the evaluated transfer scenario. This is relevant to industrial bearing prognostics, where vibration measurements collected under different operating conditions may exhibit substantial differences even when they describe comparable stages of equipment deterioration.

These results indicate that the proposed model retained a degree of resistance to moderate Gaussian noise contamination, although its prediction accuracy deteriorated substantially under stronger interference. The gradual increase in prediction errors suggests that the feature extraction and adaptation procedures continued to provide useful degradation information over the evaluated SNR range, but their ability to distinguish degradation-related responses became more limited as the noise intensity increased.

The observed behavior is consistent with the design of the DRSN-based feature extraction module. Channel-adaptive soft-thresholding was introduced to attenuate low-magnitude feature responses, while multi-scale feature fusion combined information from different network depths. The source-domain screening and subdomain alignment components were designed to reduce differences among feature representations associated with varying operating conditions. However, the present experiments do not independently establish the contribution of each component to noise resistance.

From an industrial predictive maintenance perspective, the results are relevant because bearing vibration signals are rarely collected under completely noise-free conditions. The evaluation suggests that DRSN-MW can maintain comparatively low prediction errors under moderate simulated interference, while stronger noise contamination remains a limitation.

It should also be recognized that the present robustness evaluation was based on additive white Gaussian noise. Actual industrial vibration measurements may contain impulsive interference, nonstationary disturbances, electromagnetic noise, and other forms of contamination that differ from the simulated conditions. The reported results therefore characterize robustness to the specified Gaussian noise levels rather than to all types of industrial measurement interference.

Overall, the noise robustness experiments showed a systematic relationship between signal quality and RUL prediction error. The findings provide additional evidence of the behavior of DRSN-MW under measurement disturbances and complement the cross-condition prediction results presented in the preceding sections.

sec.title: 4.3. Case 2: xi’an jiaotong university–sumyoung bearing dataset
4.3.1 Dataset description and task configuration
sec.p: To further evaluate the cross-condition RUL prediction performance of the proposed DRSN-MW framework, experiments were conducted using the XJTU-SY bearing dataset. This publicly available dataset contains vibration measurements collected throughout accelerated bearing degradation tests under different rotational speeds and mechanical loads. The dataset provides an additional experimental basis for examining the transferability of degradation representations across operating conditions.

The vibration measurements were acquired using an accelerated bearing life test platform consisting primarily of an alternating current (AC) motor, support bearings, a rotational speed controller, and acceleration sensors. The experimental arrangement is illustrated in Figure 12.

caption.title: Experimental platform used for accelerated bearing life testing in the XJTU-SY dataset

sec.p: Horizontal and vertical acceleration sensors were mounted on the bearing housing to record vibration responses during operation. LDK-UER204 bearings were used in the experiments, and their principal geometric and mechanical parameters are summarized in Table 9.

caption.title: Geometric and mechanical parameters of the bearings in the XJTU-SY dataset

sec.p: The vibration signals were acquired at a sampling frequency of 25.6 kHz, with a recording duration of 1.28 s for each acquisition and a sampling interval of 1 min. The accelerated tests continued until the specified termination criterion was reached. According to the dataset description used in this study, data acquisition was terminated when the measured acceleration amplitude exceeded 20 g, indicating an advanced fault condition.

The XJTU-SY dataset contains complete degradation records from 15 bearings tested under three operating conditions, with five bearings assigned to each condition. The operating conditions differed in rotational speed and applied load, providing distinct experimental settings for investigating cross-condition degradation prediction. The corresponding operating parameters are listed in Table 10.

caption.title: Operating conditions of the XJTU-SY bearing dataset

sec.p: The differences in rotational speed and mechanical load provided a basis for evaluating whether degradation information learned from one or more operating conditions could be transferred to another condition. In particular, the dataset allowed the proposed framework to be assessed using a different experimental platform from that employed in the PHM2012 evaluation.

Six cross-condition transfer tasks were constructed, comprising three single-source tasks and three multi-source tasks. For the single-source tasks, labeled observations from one operating condition were used to train the prediction model, while unlabeled observations from the target condition were incorporated into the domain adaptation procedure. For the multi-source tasks, labeled degradation observations from two operating conditions were available for source-domain screening and transfer learning.

In each task, the labeled source-domain training data and unlabeled target-domain adaptation data were separated from the target-domain test bearing. The target-domain test observations were reserved for performance evaluation, and their RUL labels were not used for supervised model training.
The detailed task configurations are presented in Table 11.

caption.title: Cross-condition transfer learning task configurations for the XJTU-SY dataset

sec.p: The task configurations allowed the performance of DRSN-MW to be examined under different source–target combinations. Tasks A–C assessed transfer from individual source conditions, whereas Tasks D–F examined the use of multiple source domains. The latter configuration was particularly relevant to the proposed source-domain screening mechanism, which was designed to identify degradation information more closely related to the target operating condition.

The XJTU-SY experiments therefore provided a complementary evaluation of DRSN-MW using an independent bearing degradation dataset, allowing the consistency of prediction performance across the two experimental platforms to be examined.

sec.title: 4.3.2 Analysis of remaining useful life prediction results on the xi’an jiaotong university–sumyoung dataset
sec.p: The proposed DRSN-MW framework was evaluated using the six cross-condition transfer tasks defined in Section 4.3.1. Each task was repeated independently three times, and the average prediction results were reported using MAE, RMSE, and Score. The experimental results are summarized in Table 12.

caption.title: RUL prediction performance of DRSN-MW on the XJTU-SY dataset

sec.p: The results showed that DRSN-MW maintained relatively low prediction errors across the six evaluated operating-condition combinations. The average MAE and RMSE were 0.129 and 0.156, respectively, while the average Score was 0.986. These results were close to those obtained using the PHM2012 dataset, for which the corresponding average MAE, RMSE, and Score were 0.126, 0.150, and 0.987.

Among the single-source transfer tasks, Task A produced the lowest MAE of 0.135, whereas Task B achieved the lowest RMSE of 0.159. Task C yielded the largest prediction errors, with an MAE of 0.138 and an RMSE of 0.167. These differences indicate that prediction performance varied according to the source–target operating-condition combination, even when the same transfer learning framework was applied.

The multi-source tasks produced lower prediction errors than the single-source tasks in the reported configurations. For Tasks A–C, the average MAE and RMSE were approximately 0.135 and 0.163, respectively. For Tasks D–F, the corresponding values decreased to approximately 0.122 and 0.149. These differences represented relative reductions of approximately 9.6% in MAE and 8.6% in RMSE.

Task F, which transferred degradation information from conditions C1 and C3 to C2, achieved the lowest prediction errors, with an MAE of 0.119 and an RMSE of 0.145. It also obtained the highest Score of 0.991. Task D, which used conditions C1 and C2 as source domains and C3 as the target domain, achieved an MAE of 0.122 and an RMSE of 0.149. Task E produced similarly low prediction errors, with an MAE of 0.126 and an RMSE of 0.152.

The reduction in prediction errors observed in the multi-source tasks suggests that incorporating degradation information from multiple operating conditions can improve RUL estimation when the available source data contain transferable characteristics. In the proposed DRSN-MW framework, the weighted screening procedure was designed to assess the relevance of source-domain features and degradation trajectories, while the subdomain alignment module considered differences between corresponding degradation stages.

These mechanisms may have contributed to the observed performance differences. However, the present comparison involved different combinations of source domains and target bearings, and the reported results should therefore be interpreted as evidence of performance under the evaluated configurations rather than as an isolated measurement of the contribution of source-domain screening.

A comparison of the results obtained from PHM2012 and XJTU-SY showed relatively small differences in the average evaluation metrics. The average MAE differed by 0.003, the average RMSE by 0.006, and the average Score by 0.001. This consistency indicates that DRSN-MW maintained similar levels of normalized prediction error across the two bearing datasets.

Nevertheless, the datasets differed in experimental platform, operating conditions, and bearing degradation characteristics. Similar average errors do not necessarily imply identical generalization behavior, particularly because the evaluation metrics were calculated using normalized RUL values. The results instead suggest that the proposed framework was applicable to the two evaluated accelerated bearing degradation datasets.

From an industrial predictive maintenance perspective, the XJTU-SY experiments provide additional evidence that degradation knowledge obtained under previously monitored operating conditions can be used to support RUL prediction under different loads and rotational speeds. This capability is relevant to industrial rotating machinery, where complete run-to-failure records are often unavailable for every operating condition.

Overall, the XJTU-SY results showed that DRSN-MW achieved consistent prediction performance across the evaluated transfer tasks. The findings complement the PHM2012 experiments and support further investigation of multi-source transfer learning for industrial bearing health prognostics.

sec.title: 4.3.3 Comparison with other methods
sec.p: To further examine the predictive performance of DRSN-MW on the XJTU-SY dataset, comparative experiments were reported using conventional deep learning models and transfer learning approaches. The comparison included adaptability feature perception fusion model (AFPFM), cross-residual attention transformer (CRAformer), MPA, SAUE, DRT, and DRANet.

These methods represented different approaches to feature learning and cross-domain adaptation. AFPFM and CRAformer were included as deep learning comparison models, while MPA, SAUE, DRT, and DRANet provided transfer learning references. The latter approaches were originally developed for broader domain adaptation problems and were considered here in the context of bearing RUL prediction.
The original experimental description identified Task D as the representative transfer scenario selected for comparison. The reported results are presented in Table 13.

caption.title: Comparative RUL prediction results on the XJTU-SY dataset

sec.p: The reported results showed that DRSN-MW achieved the lowest MAE and RMSE among the evaluated methods. Its MAE was 0.133 and its RMSE was 0.159, while the corresponding Score reached 0.984.

Among the conventional deep learning models, AFPFM produced an MAE of 0.347 and an RMSE of 0.404, whereas CRAformer achieved an MAE of 0.324 and an RMSE of 0.387. The transfer learning approaches generally produced lower prediction errors than these two models under the reported comparison conditions.

Among the transfer learning methods, DRANet achieved the lowest MAE and RMSE, with values of 0.183 and 0.231, respectively. Compared with DRANet, DRSN-MW reduced MAE by approximately 27.3% and RMSE by 31.2%. The Score increased from 0.959 to 0.984, corresponding to an absolute increase of 0.025.

The differences between the methods are consistent with the importance of accounting for distribution discrepancies when transferring degradation information across operating conditions. Conventional feature learning methods may capture useful vibration characteristics but do not necessarily account for differences between source and target distributions. Domain adaptation approaches address this problem by incorporating mechanisms intended to reduce such discrepancies.

The proposed DRSN-MW framework combined source-domain screening, degradation-stage-aware feature alignment, and constrained regression within a unified prediction architecture. The screening procedure evaluated source-domain relevance, while the entropy-weighted LMMD module considered distribution differences between corresponding degradation stages. Decision consistency and physical monotonicity regularization were further introduced to control the behavior of the regression outputs.

These components provide possible explanations for the lower prediction errors observed in the reported comparison. Nevertheless, the contribution of each mechanism cannot be established from Table 13 alone and should be interpreted together with the ablation results presented in Section 4.2.4.

When considered alongside the PHM2012 results, the XJTU-SY comparison suggests that DRSN-MW can produce lower normalized RUL prediction errors than the evaluated approaches under the reported experimental conditions. The findings support the relevance of multi-source transfer learning and degradation-stage alignment to bearing health prognostics, while further evaluation under variable industrial operating conditions remains necessary.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: This study developed a multi-source weighted transfer learning framework, termed DRSN-MW, for RUL prediction of rolling bearings under different operating conditions. The framework integrated a DRSN with adaptive threshold adjustment, extension-based source-domain screening, degradation-stage-aware subdomain alignment, and physically constrained regression. Entropy-weighted DTW was employed to assess the similarity of degradation trajectories across operating conditions, while Mix-up-based feature recombination and entropy-weighted LMMD were introduced to reduce distribution discrepancies between corresponding degradation stages. Decision consistency regularization and physical monotonicity constraints were further incorporated to regulate the predicted RUL trajectories. These components were designed to address the combined effects of heterogeneous degradation patterns, source-domain differences, and prediction inconsistency in cross-condition bearing prognostics.

The proposed framework was evaluated using the PHM2012 and XJTU-SY bearing datasets under single-source and multi-source transfer scenarios. On the PHM2012 dataset, DRSN-MW achieved average MAE and RMSE values of 0.126 and 0.150, respectively, with an average Score of 0.987. Compared with DRANet, the strongest comparison method in terms of average prediction error, the proposed framework reduced MAE by 29.2% and RMSE by 33.6%. On the XJTU-SY dataset, average MAE and RMSE values of 0.129 and 0.156 were obtained, respectively, with an average Score of 0.986. The multi-source transfer tasks generally produced lower prediction errors than the single-source tasks on both datasets. The ablation results further showed that the complete DRSN-MW configuration achieved lower prediction errors than the evaluated partial configurations. In addition, the noise robustness experiments indicated that prediction accuracy was relatively stable under moderate Gaussian noise contamination, although larger errors were observed at lower SNRs.

The results indicate that combining source-domain screening, degradation-stage alignment, and physical constraints is a useful approach to cross-condition bearing RUL prediction. By transferring degradation information from previously monitored operating conditions, the proposed framework provides a basis for predictive maintenance of industrial rotating machinery when labeled run-to-failure data are limited for the target condition. Nevertheless, the present evaluation was based on accelerated bearing degradation datasets, and the effects of continuously varying operating conditions, different machinery configurations, and complex industrial measurement noise remain to be investigated. Further validation using operational monitoring data is therefore required to establish the applicability of DRSN-MW to industrial maintenance systems.
